newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Debt plan seen as first of Ivorian Caistab reforms.
newsitem.headline: Debt plan seen as first of Ivorian Caistab reforms.

text.p: Ivory Coast's transfer of debt management for its Caistab commodities board to the Treasury could mark the start of wider Caistab reforms urged by donors, industry analysts said on Friday.

The Treasury was named to take over management of public debt and operations co-funded by donors from the state Caisse Autonome d'Amortissement (CAA) during a cabinet decision on Thursday, a statement issued afterwards said.

Donors, due to hold a meeting in mid-August with Ivory Coast on drawing up a three-year economic policy plan, have linked liberalisation of the Caistab to a $150 million agriculture loan dating to 1995. Cocoa and coffee reforms are on the agenda.
"We are on a path. We do not know how long it will be but coffee is set for liberalisation in 1998/99 (Oct-Sept)," said one analayst. "Cocoa, on the other hand, will be a tough battle.
"It looks like a start but there is a lot to be done before the donors will be satisfied," he added.
Donors say a tentative date for liberalisation of cocoa has been set for 1999/2000, although many details remained to be resolved.
The Caistab until 1995 exercised a monopoly on cocoa and coffee marketing and wants to retain a role in produce price-setting, export rights auctioning and quality assurance.
In 1996/97 it issued "reference" minimum farmgate prices for coffee and cocoa, rather than fixed rates under a list of marketing prices from farms to ports until then set for each season.
Donors want an end to all types of state price-setting, which they say would lead to a question mark over the need to sell forward two-thirds of each year's crop before seaons open.
"Exporters would then play the role they are used to. Buying and selling rather than acting as an agent for the government," said the analyst.

The World Bank has pushed for a free market to help raise prices paid by buyers to farmers -- rejecting fears that a free market would mean plummeting bean quality. --Matthew Bunce, Abidjan newsroom + 225 219090
